WHAT CHANGED FROM YEAR 1: the Letter of Interest phase has been REMOVED, so this is a single direct application. FOCUS AREAS: alongside an open call for projects aligned to any of Alaska's six RHTP Initiatives, the fall cycle names three focus areas - EMS Implementation Pathway (emergency medical services, emergency response); Care Coordination Implementation Pathway (hospital discharges, transitions between care settings, or follow-up care after hospitalization); and Pay for Value Readiness Implementation Pathway (value-based payment arrangements, population health management, or other approaches that reward quality, outcomes, or coordinated care). OUT-OF-STATE APPLICANTS ARE EXPLICITLY ALLOWED. The RHTP Organization-Level Eligibility document states: 'Organizations may be based anywhere in the United States, provided the proposed project demonstrably benefits rural Alaskans and aligns with Alaska's RHTP initiatives. It is strongly recommended that organizations based outside of Alaska partner with Alaskan organizations or articulate a clear connection to Alaska.' Eligible organization types include 'Nonprofit organizations and community-based organizations', 'Social service providers and community health organizations' and 'Technology, innovation, or service partners working in collaboration with eligible Alaska-based entities'. To be eligible an applicant must be a legally established organization (not an individual), have legal authority to enter a subaward agreement, comply with federal grant requirements, and 'Obtain and maintain a Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) and register in SAM.gov prior to award issuance'. Ineligible: individuals and sole proprietors, debarred or excluded entities, and organizations that cannot meet 2 CFR Part 200 administrative, financial or compliance requirements. Geography is not a barrier either: 'Organizations anywhere in Alaska will be able to apply... Projects based in urban areas can improve rural health outcomes.'

THE BIG CHANGE: THE LONG-OVERDUE CRITICAL ACCESS HOSPITAL & ACUTE CARE HOSPITAL RFA POSTED ON OCT 1, 2026, AND IT IS OPEN TO OUT-OF-STATE LEAD APPLICANTS. This is the most important development in New Hampshire since the Primary Care RFA, because its eligibility rules are materially more permissive than the Primary Care RFA's. Section 2.1 lists four lead-applicant types: NH Critical Access Hospitals; NH licensed hospitals without CAH designation located in a rural area; NH licensed hospitals not in a rural area but proposing a project directed at and predominantly impacting rural NH patients; and - the open door - 'Organizations partnering with an eligible applicant to transform the delivery of hospital care in rural New Hampshire.' The RFA then states plainly: 'Applicants are not required to be located in New Hampshire. An applicant located outside the State must clearly demonstrate how the proposed project will directly deliver services to, expand healthcare capacity for, or otherwise benefit rural New Hampshire hospitals, patients, and communities.' There is no Primary Care Alignment Test and no NH-partners-only restriction in this RFA.

CAH & ACUTE CARE HOSPITAL RFA DETAIL: initial grant term from contract execution through Sept 30, 2027 (Budget Period 1), with non-competitive continuation funding possible in later budget periods contingent on GO-NORTH authorization. No stated ceiling or total pool on the RFA face. Application portal opens late October 2026; initial Priority Cohort deadline Nov 12, 2026 at 5:00 PM ET ('Guaranteed to be scored against available funding as part of the initial cohort'); initial-cohort notification mid-December 2026; rolling applications accepted after the initial deadline and reviewed in order received subject to remaining funding, with notification within 45-60 days. Information session 'Details and registration TBD.' Three readiness stages (Project Development, Preparatory Investments, Program Ready) - applicants are explicitly not penalised for starting at an earlier stage. Three Focus Areas; at least one is required. Focus Area 1 ACCESS is the Vivo-relevant one: 'Transforming care delivery approaches, including telehealth and expanded specialty access; sustainable emergency department transformation; obstetric service sustainability; hospital-at-home and post-acute optimization; care coordination and supporting technology; outpatient service expansion; and other applicant-proposed care models that demonstrate a direct benefit to rural New Hampshire communities.' Application limits: unlimited applications at Project Development stage; one application as lead applicant at Preparatory Investments or Program Ready, but 'There is no limitation on the number of applications an organization can participate as a partner or subrecipient in applications submitted by another organization as the lead applicant.' Narrative is short: 600 words rationale, 1,200 words focus-area response, 2,000 words project plan and capacity, 400 words rural impact. Combined indirect and administrative costs capped at 10% of total funding requested, regardless of any federally negotiated rate. Equipment over $10,000 per unit needs prior written FHC approval and retroactive approval requests will not be considered. Ineligible: free-standing EDs, activities duplicating existing GO-NORTH work, research including clinical trials and secondary data analysis, lobbying, workforce activities giving a direct cash benefit to an employee, and organizations that helped design the RFA (2 CFR 200.318(c)). TWO NEW FHC GUIDANCE DOCUMENTS, BOTH OCT 2026. (1) 'Funding Direct Health Care Services (Provider Payments)' confirms RHT funds may pay for health care items or services not covered by insurance where they address a documented rural care gap, but caps provider payments under CMS Use-of-Funds Category B at 15% of New Hampshire's total CMS award in a budget period, and states 'There is no pre-approved list of clinical service lines.' The scope is squarely Vivo's language: the fund backs organizations 'that have a novel healthcare technology solution that push boundaries and address barriers in advancing consumer-facing, technology-driven solutions for chronic disease prevention and management in rural populations that are currently unavailable and/or unattainable through traditional funding structures', and 'Preference will be given to solutions that directly deliver or enable care.' THE MATURITY GATE IS THE REAL RISK ON THE TECH INNOVATION FUND, NOT GEOGRAPHY. The product must 'be between proof-of-concept and minimum viable product. This represents Technical Readiness Levels four through seven', and the RFA states 'A product will be considered too mature if it is fully commercialized with a focus on marketing and sales.' Proof-of-concept criteria require a functional prototype, evidence or demonstration of feasibility, and demonstrated readiness. The applicant must also be 'an entity founded less than 10 years ago and with less than $50M prior funding raised since the organization's inception' and hold a UEI active in SAM.gov with no exclusions. Vivo should settle internally whether it reads as MVP-stage or as a commercialized service before spending on an application - this is the same gate that applies to the Delaware and Louisiana Catalyst Funds, and the answer should be consistent across all three.
